## Custom Functions

We now build some custom functions required for the analyses. Note that here you can find the syntax for the main analyses wrapped in helper functions, which we will then call below.

```{r}
# define function to silence result output
# needed for brms
hush <- 
  function(
    code
    ){
    sink("/dev/null") # use /dev/null in UNIX
    tmp = code
    sink()
    return(tmp)
    }

# plot distributions of items
plot_dist <-
  function(
    item,
    n_rows = 1
    ) {
    ggplot(
      gather(
        select(
          d, 
          starts_with(
            item
            )
          )
        ), 
      mapping = aes(
        x = value
        )
      ) +
      geom_bar() +
      facet_wrap(
        ~key, 
        nrow = n_rows
        ) + 
      theme_bw()
  }

get_desc <- 
  function(
    item,
    name
  ) {
    desc <- 
      select(
        d, 
        starts_with(
          item
          )
        ) %>% 
      apply(
        1, 
        mean, 
        na.rm = TRUE
        ) %>% 
      as.data.frame() %>% 
      summarise(
        m = mean(., na.rm = TRUE), 
        sd = sd(., na.rm = TRUE)
        )
    assign(
      paste0(
        "des_",
        name
      ),
      desc,
      envir = .GlobalEnv
    )
  }

# Function to display diagnostics of fitted hurdle models
model_diagnostics <- 
  function(
    model
  ){
  plot_grid(
    pp_check(
      model,
      type = "dens_overlay",
      nsamples = 100
    ),
    pp_check(
      model,
      type = "loo_pit_qq",
      nsamples = 100
    ),
    pp_check(
      model,
      type = "stat",
      stat = "median",
      nsamples = 100
    ),
    pp_check(
      model,
      type = "stat",
      stat = "mean",
      nsamples = 100
    ),
    labels = c("Density overlay", "LOO-PIT QQ", "Predicted medians", "Predicted means"),
    ncol = 2,
    label_size = 8,
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 0,
    label_x = 0,
    label_y = 0.93
    )
  }

# wrapper function that runs relevant analyses for hurdle models
run_hurdles <- 
  function(
    object,
    name,
    outcome,
    predictor,
    x_lab,
    y_lab,
    plot = FALSE,
    ...
    ){
    
    # define define general model
    formula_mdl <- 
      formula(
        paste0(
          outcome,
          " ~ 1 + age + male + edu +",
          predictor
        )
    )
    
    # define hurdle model
    formula_hrdl <- 
      formula(
        paste0(
          "hu ~ 1 + age + male + edu +",
          predictor
        )
    )
   
    # fit model
    fit <- 
      hush(
        brms::brm(
          bf(
            formula_mdl, 
            formula_hrdl
            ), 
          data = object, 
          family = hurdle_gamma(),
          silent = TRUE,
          refresh = 0,
          iter = 1000,
          backend = "rstan"
          )
      )
    
    # export fit
    assign(
      paste0(
        "fit_",
        name),
      fit,
      envir = .GlobalEnv
    )
    
    # plot model
    if(
      isTRUE(plot
             )) {
      plot(fit, ask = FALSE)
  }
    
    # run diagnostics
    fit_diagnostics <- 
      model_diagnostics(fit)
    plot(fit_diagnostics)
    
    # print summary
    fit_summary <- 
      summary(fit)
    print(fit_summary)

    # calculate slopes
    slopes <-
      cbind(
        Outcome = outcome,
        avg_slopes(fit)
      )
    
    # print slopes
    cat("\nResults of marginal effects:\n")
    print(slopes)
    
    # export as object to environment
    assign(
      paste0(
        "slopes_",
        name
        ),
      slopes,
      envir = .GlobalEnv
    )
    
    # make figure
    fig_res <- 
      conditional_effects(
        fit
        , ask = FALSE
      )
    
    # make figure
    fig <- 
      plot(
        fig_res,
        plot = FALSE
      )[[predictor]] +
      labs(
        x = x_lab,
        y = y_lab
        )
    
    # plot figure
    print(fig)
    
    # export as object to environment
    assign(
      paste0(
        "fig_",
        name
      ),
      fig,
      envir = .GlobalEnv
    )
}
```

## Sample

### Speeders

We filtered participants who answered the questionnaire in less than three minutes, which we considered to be unreasonably fast.

```{r cache=F}
# filter speeders
time_crit <- 3 # minimum time on survey

# count number of speeders
n_speeding <- 
  nrow(
    filter(
      d, 
      time_sum_min_t2 < time_crit
      )
    )

# Deletion of fast respondents
d <- 
  filter(
    d, 
    time_sum_min_t2 >= time_crit
    )
```

### Response Patterns

We inspected the data manually for cases with obvious response patterns. The following cases show extreme response patterns (alongside fast response times), and were hence removed.

```{r cache=F}

d %>%
```

## Self-Disclosure Index

We construct the self-disclosure index here, after the final sample has been determined, because the standardization depends on the sample.
Following @omarzuDisclosureDecisionModel2000, self-disclosure consists of three dimensions: quantity (number of words), breadth (average number of topics per comment, 0–3), and depth (average number of disclosure markers per comment: personal experience + emotional expression + political opinion, 0–3).
Breadth and depth stem from the LLM coding of all comments (see `04c_final_classification.ipynb`).
Participants who did not comment get 0 on all three dimensions.

Each dimension is z-standardized and then linearly transformed so that its lowest value is 0.
The index is the mean of the three transformed dimensions, which is again standardized and transformed so that its lowest value is 0.
Participants who did not comment hence have a value of exactly 0 (which the hurdle models require), and all other values are expressed in standard deviations.

```{r sd-indicators, cache=F}
# LLM codes per comment, aggregated per person
comments_coded <- read_csv("data/comments/final/comments_classified_final.csv")

sd_components <-
  comments_coded %>%
  filter(!is.na(id)) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(
    breadth_mean = mean(breadth, na.rm = TRUE),   # 0-3, mean topics per comment
    depth_mean   = mean(depth, na.rm = TRUE)      # 0-3, mean of pers_exp + emot_exp + pol_opin
    )

# z-standardize, then shift so that the lowest value is 0
z_min0 <- function(x) {
  z <- as.numeric(scale(x))
  z - min(z)
  }

d <-
  d %>%
  select(-any_of(c("breadth_mean", "depth_mean"))) %>%
  left_join(sd_components, by = "id") %>%
  mutate(
    # non-commenters disclosed nothing
    across(c(breadth_mean, depth_mean), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)),
    sd_quantity = z_min0(words),
    sd_breadth  = z_min0(breadth_mean),
    sd_depth    = z_min0(depth_mean)
    )
```

```{r sd-index, cache=F}
d <-
  d %>%
  mutate(
    self_disc = (sd_quantity + sd_breadth + sd_depth) / 3,
    self_disc = (self_disc - min(self_disc)) / sd(self_disc)
    )

# checks: non-commenters exactly 0, all commenters above 0
stopifnot(all(d$self_disc[d$words == 0] == 0))
stopifnot(all(d$self_disc[d$words > 0] > 0))
```

# Measures

Let's next inspect all measures. We list all items, their distributions and CFAs.

## Privacy concerns
### Items

Using the participation platform I had ...

 1. ... concerns about what happens to my data.
 2. ... concerns about disclosing information about myself.
 3. ... no concerns. (reversed)
 4. ... concerns that others could discover my real identity (i.e. my last and first name).
 5. ... concerns that information about myself could fall into wrong hands.
 6. ... concerns that others could discover what my political views are.
 7. ... concerns about my privacy.

### Distributions

```{r fig.height = 3}
# plot distribution
plot_dist(
  item = "PC01"
)

# extract results
get_desc(
  item = "PC01",
  name = "pricon"
)
```

### CFA

```{r}
name <- "pricon"
model <- "
pri_con =~ PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_03 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07
"
fit <- 
  lavaan::sem(
    model = model, 
    data = d, 
    estimator = "MLR", 
    missing = "ML"
    )
```

Model fit:

```{r}
facval <- 
  fit_tab(
    fit, 
    # reliability = TRUE, 
    # scaled = TRUE
    ) %T>%
  print()
```

Factor loadings:

```{r}
inspect(
  fit,
  what = "std") %$% 
    lambda
```

Shows that PC01_03 doesn't load well. As it's an inverted item that's not surprising. Also from a theoretic perspective it's suboptimal, because it doesn't explicitly focus on privacy, but just concerns in general. Will be deleted.

## Trust general
### Items


### CFA

Note that we constrained two loadings to be able to report model fit. We used operators and website, as these are theoretically closer.

```{r}
name <- "trustgen"
model <- "
trust =~ TR02_01 + a*TR02_02 + a*TR02_03
"
fit <- 
  lavaan::sem(
    model = model, 
    data = d, 
    estimator = "MLR", 
    missing = "ML"
    )
```

Model fit:

```{r}
facval <- 
  fit_tab(
    fit, 
    # reliability = TRUE, 
    # scaled = TRUE
    ) %T>%
  print()

assign(
  paste0(
    name, 
    "_facval"
    ), 
  facval
  )
```

Factor loadings:

```{r}
inspect(
  fit,
  what = "std"
  ) %$%
  lambda
```

Note that we constrained Items 5 and 9 to be equal. Explanation: First, they are theoretically related. Second, not constraining would yield to just-identified model, for which model fit cannot be interpreted meaningfully.

## Self-disclosure

Self-disclosure was computed above (see Setup) as an index of three dimensions: quantity (number of words), breadth, and depth.
Because the index consists of only three dimensions, a confirmatory factor analysis would be just identified and not informative; we hence report no CFA, but the dimensions, their correlations, and the distribution of the index.

## Baseline Model

In what follows, please find the results of all variables combined in one model. This model will be used to extract factor scores.

```{r cache=F}
model_baseline <- "
  pri_con =~ PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07
  grats_gen =~ GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05
  grats_inf =~ GR01_01 + GR01_02 + GR01_03 
  grats_rel =~ GR01_04 + GR01_05 + GR01_06 
  grats_par =~ GR01_07 + GR01_08 + GR01_09
  grats_ide =~ GR01_10 + GR01_11 + GR01_12 
  grats_ext =~ GR01_13 + GR01_14 + GR01_15
  grats_spec =~ grats_inf + grats_rel + grats_par + grats_ide + grats_ext
  pri_delib =~ PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05
  trust_gen =~ TR02_01 + TR02_02 + TR02_03
  trust_community =~ TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03
  trust_provider =~ TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06
  trust_system =~ TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09
  trust_spec =~ trust_community + trust_provider + trust_system
  self_eff =~ SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04
    SE01_01 ~~ x*SE01_02
    SE01_03 ~~ x*SE01_04
  Words_log =~ words_log
  
  Words_log ~~ a1*pri_con + b1*grats_gen + c1*pri_delib + d1*self_eff + e1*trust_spec + f1*trust_gen + g1*grats_spec
"

fit_baseline <- 
  lavaan::sem(
    model_baseline, 
    data = d, 
    missing = "ML"
    )

summary(
  fit_baseline, 
  standardized = TRUE, 
  fit.measures = TRUE
  )
```

```{r cache=F}
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  mutate(
    version = d$version, 
    grats_gen_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("GR02"))),
    grats_spec_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("GR01"))), 
    pri_con_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("PC01"))),
    trust_gen_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("TR02"))),
    trust_spec_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("TR01"))),
    pri_del_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("PD01"))),
    self_eff_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("SE01"))),
    self_disc = d$self_disc) %>%
  select(
    version, 
    pri_con_fs, 
    grats_gen_fs, 
    grats_spec_fs, 
    pri_del_fs, 
    self_eff_fs, 
    trust_gen_fs, 
    trust_spec_fs,

  cbind(

      -version, 
      -words_log,
```

# Power Analyses

In what follows, we report power analyses for our study. Please note that we conduct a rudimentary power analysis, assuming bivariate correlations. (At the time, we were not yet aware of the existence of power analyses for multivariate structural equation models.)

```{r include=F}
# define pwr-criteria
z_crit <- 1.96
alpha <- .05
power_desired <- .95
r_sesoi <- .10
```

We first estimate the sample size necessary to find small effects in 95% of all cases.

```{r}
# estimate pwr-samplesize
pwr.r.test(
  r = r_sesoi, 
  sig.level = alpha, 
  power = power_desired, 
  alternative = "greater"
  ) %T>%
  print %$% 
  n %>% 
  round(0) ->
  n_desired
```

We then compute the power we have achieved with our final sample size to detect small effects.

```{r}
# compute pwr-achieved
pwr.r.test(
  n = n_final, 
  r = r_sesoi, 
  sig.level = alpha, 
  alternative = "greater"
  ) %T>%
  print %$% 
  power %>% 
  round(2) ->
  power_achieved
```

We finally compute what effect size we are likely to find in 95% of all cases given our final sample size.

```{r}
# estimate pwr-sensitivity
pwr.r.test(
  n = n_final, 
  power = power_desired, 
  sig.level = alpha, 
  alternative = "greater"
  ) %T>%
  print %$% 
  r %>% 
  round(2) ->
  r_sensitive
```

## Privacy Calculus

```{r}
model <- "
  pri_con =~ PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 
  grats_gen =~ GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05

  self_eff =~ SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04
  SE01_01 ~~ x*SE01_02
  SE01_03 ~~ x*SE01_04
  trust_community =~ TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03
  trust_provider =~ TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06
  trust_system =~ TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09
  
  trust_spec =~ trust_community + trust_provider + trust_system

words_log ~ a1*pri_con + b1*grats_gen + c1*pri_delib + d1*self_eff + e1*trust_spec

# Covariates
words_log + GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05 + PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 + TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03 + TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06 + TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09 + PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05 + SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04 ~ male + age + edu

# Covariances
male ~~ age + edu
age ~~ edu
"

fit_prereg <- 
  lavaan::sem(
    model, 
    data = d, 
    estimator = "MLR", 
    missing = "ML"
    )

summary(
  fit_prereg, 
  fit = TRUE, 
  std = TRUE
  )

rsquare_fit_prereg <- 
  inspect(
    fit_prereg, 
    what = "rsquare"
    )["words"]
```

Results show that there's only one significant predictor of Communication, being self-efficacy. The other predictors are in the direction as planned, albeit not significant. Trust, however, shows the inverse relation as effect, that is, more trust, less communication.

# Exploratory Analyses

## Rationale

The bivariate relations showed several strong correlations. 
People who trusted the providers more also experienced more gratifications (_r_ = .79).
In multiple regression, we analyze the potential effect of one variable on the outcome while holding all others constant. 
In this case, we tested whether trust increases communication while holding constant gratifications, privacy concerns, privacy deliberations, and self-efficacy. 
Given the close theoretical and empirical interrelations between the predictors, this creates an unlikely and artificial scenario. 
If people lose trust in a provider, they will likely experience more concerns and less benefits. 
But it is not even necessary to control for these mediating factors. 
When trying to analyze the causal effect, it is necessary to control for confounding variables, but importantly not for mediators [@rohrerThinkingClearlyCorrelations2018].
Confounding variables impact both the independent variable and the outcome. 
Sociodemographic variables are often ideal candidates for confounders.
For example, men are generally less concerned about their privacy and post more online.
Hence, controlling for gender helps isolate the actual causal effect. 
As a result, we reran the analyses controlling for confounding variables that are not mediators.

## Communication

In what follows, we analyze the preregistered outcome, communication, measured as the number of words a participant wrote.
All privacy calculus variables are standardized (_z_-scores), so that effects refer to an increase of one standard deviation.

### Experimental Factors

We first compare likes and likes plus dislikes to the control condition.

```{r wrds-ctrl}
run_hurdles(
  object = d,
  name = "wrds_ctrl",
  outcome = "words",
  predictor = "version",
  y_lab = "Words",
  x_lab = "Experimental conditions"
  )
```

Let's find out by how much people in the like and like plus dislike conditions wrote fewer words.

```{r wrds-ctrl-effects}
words_m_ctrl   <- fig_wrds_ctrl$data %>% filter(effect1__ == "Control") %>% pull(estimate__)
words_m_lk     <- fig_wrds_ctrl$data %>% filter(effect1__ == "Like") %>% pull(estimate__)
words_m_lkdslk <- fig_wrds_ctrl$data %>% filter(effect1__ == "Like & dislike") %>% pull(estimate__)

effect_lk_prcnt    <- round((words_m_ctrl - words_m_lk) / words_m_ctrl * 100)
effect_lkdlk_prcnt <- round((words_m_ctrl - words_m_lkdslk) / words_m_ctrl * 100)
```

Compared to the control condition, participants wrote `r effect_lkdlk_prcnt` percent fewer words on the platform with likes and dislikes, and `r effect_lk_prcnt` percent fewer words on the platform with likes only.

We then compare the likes and control conditions to the likes plus dislikes condition.

```{r wrds-lkdslk}
run_hurdles(
  object = d,
  name = "wrds_lkdslk",
  outcome = "words",
  predictor = "version_lkdslk",
  y_lab = "Words",
  x_lab = "Experimental conditions"
  )
```

### Privacy Concerns

```{r wrds-pricon}
run_hurdles(
  object = d,
  name = "wrds_pricon",
  outcome = "words",
  predictor = "pri_con_z",
  y_lab = "Words",
  x_lab = "Privacy concerns (z)"
  )
```

Let's explore how the number of communicated words differs between people with the lowest and the highest privacy concerns in our sample.

```{r wrds-pricon-effects}
wrds_pricon_1 <- fig_wrds_pricon$data %>% filter(pri_con_z == min(pri_con_z)) %>% pull(estimate__) %>% round(0)
wrds_pricon_7 <- fig_wrds_pricon$data %>% filter(pri_con_z == max(pri_con_z)) %>% pull(estimate__) %>% round(0)
```

People with the lowest privacy concerns communicated on average `r wrds_pricon_1` words, whereas people with the highest privacy concerns communicated on average `r wrds_pricon_7` words.

### Privacy Deliberation

### Self-Efficacy

```{r wrds-selfeff}
run_hurdles(
  object = d,
  name = "wrds_selfeff",
  outcome = "words",
  predictor = "self_eff_z",
  y_lab = "Words",
  x_lab = "Self-efficacy (z)"
  )
```

The relation is markedly exponential. Let's inspect how the number of words changes with a one-SD increase in self-efficacy, once starting from the lowest level of self-efficacy in our sample, and once ending at the highest level.

```{r wrds-selfeff-effects}
self_eff_lo <- min(d$self_eff_z)       # lowest observed self-efficacy
self_eff_hi <- max(d$self_eff_z) - 1   # one SD below the highest observed self-efficacy

# average change in the expected number of words for a one-SD increase,
# evaluated for all participants at the given level of self-efficacy (counterfactual grid)
effects_wrds_selfeff_12 <-
  avg_comparisons(
    fit_wrds_selfeff,
    variables = list(self_eff_z = 1),
    newdata = datagrid(self_eff_z = self_eff_lo, grid_type = "counterfactual")
    ) %>%
  pull(estimate) %>%
  round(0)

effects_wrds_selfeff_67 <-
  avg_comparisons(
    fit_wrds_selfeff,
    variables = list(self_eff_z = 1),
    newdata = datagrid(self_eff_z = self_eff_hi, grid_type = "counterfactual")
    ) %>%
  pull(estimate) %>%
  round(0)
```

Starting from the lowest level of self-efficacy, an increase of one standard deviation was associated with `r effects_wrds_selfeff_12` more words; ending at the highest level, the same increase was associated with `r effects_wrds_selfeff_67` more words.

Let's explore how the number of communicated words differs between people with the lowest and the highest self-efficacy in our sample.

```{r wrds-selfeff-minmax}
wrds_selfeff_1 <- fig_wrds_selfeff$data %>% filter(self_eff_z == min(self_eff_z)) %>% pull(estimate__) %>% round(0)
wrds_selfeff_7 <- fig_wrds_selfeff$data %>% filter(self_eff_z == max(self_eff_z)) %>% pull(estimate__) %>% round(0)
```

People with the lowest self-efficacy communicated on average `r wrds_selfeff_1` words, whereas people with the highest self-efficacy communicated on average `r wrds_selfeff_7` words.

### Table

Table of the average marginal effects (words: rounded to whole words).

```{r wrds-tab}
# helper: turn the slopes of several hurdle models into one table
label_slopes <- function(slopes_list) {

  predictors <- c(
    "pri_con_z"    = "Privacy concerns",
    "pri_del_z"    = "Privacy deliberation",
    "grats_gen_z"  = "Expected gratifications",
    "trust_gen_z"  = "Trust",
    "self_eff_z"   = "Self-efficacy",
    "Like - Control"           = "Like vs. control",
    "Like & dislike - Control" = "Like & dislike vs. control",
    "Like - Like & dislike"    = "Like vs. like & dislike"
    )

  outcomes <- c(
    "pri_con_fs"   = "Privacy concerns",
    "pri_del_fs"   = "Privacy deliberation",
    "grats_gen_fs" = "Expected gratifications",
    "trust_gen_fs" = "Trust",
    "self_eff_fs"  = "Self-efficacy"
    )

  slopes_list %>%
    map(as.data.frame) %>%
    bind_rows() %>%
    mutate(
      # for the experimental factors, the contrast identifies the comparison
      term = if_else(
        contrast %in% c("Like - Control", "Like & dislike - Control", "Like - Like & dislike"),
        contrast,
        term
        )
      ) %>%
    filter(term %in% names(predictors)) %>%   # drops the covariates and the duplicated contrast
    mutate(
      Predictor = factor(
        predictors[term], 
        levels = c("Self-efficacy", "Trust", "Privacy deliberation", "Expected gratifications", 
                   "Privacy concerns", "Like vs. like & dislike", "Like & dislike vs. control", 
                   "Like vs. control")
        ),
      Outcome   = recode(Outcome, !!!outcomes),
      Estimate  = if_else(Outcome == "words", round(estimate), estimate),
      LL        = if_else(Outcome == "words", round(conf.low), conf.low),
      UL        = if_else(Outcome == "words", round(conf.high), conf.high)
      ) %>%
    select(Outcome, Predictor, Estimate, LL, UL)
}

tab_slopes <-
  label_slopes(
    list(
      slopes_wrds_pricon,
      slopes_wrds_grats,
      slopes_wrds_pridel,
      slopes_wrds_trust,
      slopes_wrds_selfeff,
      slopes_wrds_ctrl,
      slopes_wrds_lkdslk,
      slopes_pricon_ctrl,
      slopes_pricon_lkdslk,
      slopes_grats_ctrl,
      slopes_grats_lkdslk,
      slopes_pridel_ctrl,
      slopes_pridel_lkdslk,
      slopes_trust_ctrl,
      slopes_trust_lkdslk,
      slopes_selfeff_ctrl,
      slopes_selfeff_lkdslk
      )
    )

tab_slopes %>%
  kable(digits = 2) %>%
  kable_styling("striped") %>%
  scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

## Self-Disclosure

How do the results change if we look at self-disclosure instead of communication only?
Self-disclosure is the standardized index described above (see Measures): 0 means that someone did not disclose anything (did not comment), and all other values are expressed in standard deviations.
Predictors are again standardized, so effects can be read as the change in self-disclosure (in SD) for a one-SD increase in the predictor.

### Experimental Factors

We first compare likes and likes plus dislikes to the control condition.

```{r sd-ctrl}
run_hurdles(
  object = d,
  name = "self_disc_ctrl",
  outcome = "self_disc",
  predictor = "version",
  y_lab = "Self-disclosure",
  x_lab = "Experimental conditions"
  )
```

```{r sd-ctrl-effects}
sd_m_ctrl   <- fig_self_disc_ctrl$data %>% filter(effect1__ == "Control") %>% pull(estimate__)
sd_m_lk     <- fig_self_disc_ctrl$data %>% filter(effect1__ == "Like") %>% pull(estimate__)
sd_m_lkdslk <- fig_self_disc_ctrl$data %>% filter(effect1__ == "Like & dislike") %>% pull(estimate__)

effect_lk_prcnt_sd    <- round((sd_m_ctrl - sd_m_lk) / sd_m_ctrl * 100)
effect_lkdlk_prcnt_sd <- round((sd_m_ctrl - sd_m_lkdslk) / sd_m_ctrl * 100)
```

Compared to the control condition, self-disclosure was `r effect_lkdlk_prcnt_sd` percent lower on the platform with likes and dislikes, and `r effect_lk_prcnt_sd` percent lower on the platform with likes only.

We then compare the likes and control conditions to the likes plus dislikes condition.

## Communication vs. Self-Disclosure

The average marginal effects for both outcomes side by side: communication (number of words) and self-disclosure (in SD).

```{r tab-wide}
tab_slopes_wide <- 
  bind_rows(
    tab_slopes %>% filter(Outcome == "words"),
    tab_slopes_self_disc %>% filter(Outcome == "self_disc")
    ) %>% 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Outcome, 
    values_from = c(Estimate, LL, UL), 
    names_glue = "{Outcome}_{.value}"
    ) %>% 
  select(
    Predictor, 
    words_Estimate, words_LL, words_UL, 
    self_disc_Estimate, self_disc_LL, self_disc_UL
    ) %>% 
  arrange(desc(Predictor))

tab_slopes_wide %>% 
  kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Predictor", "Estimate", "LL", "UL", "Estimate", "LL", "UL")
    ) %>% 
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Communication (words)" = 3, "Self-disclosure (SD)" = 3)) %>% 
  kable_styling("striped") %>% 
  scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

All average marginal effects in one long table, including the effects of the popularity cues on the privacy calculus variables.
